10884-a-publisher-and-his-friends-memoir:
Samuel Smiles's memoir of John Murray, condensed and edited by Thomas Mackay in 1911, tells the story of the great publishing house from 1768 to 1843. The first John Murray, an officer of marines turned bookseller, bought Sandby's business and built a list through letters, quarrels, and friendships. His son, the second John Murray, carried the firm to fame.

The memoir prints correspondence with authors, booksellers, and men of letters, showing how books were made and sold. Portraits illustrate the volume. Readers interested in publishing get an insider's history of the house that published Byron, Scott, and Darwin's age.
57173-a-yankee-girl-at-shiloh:
Alice Turner Curtis wrote A Yankee Girl at Shiloh, issued in Philadelphia in nineteen twenty-two. Isabel W Caley drew the pictures. Curtis had written A Yankee Girl at Fort Sumter and A Yankee Girl at Bull Run. Her Little Maid's Historical Series had made her name with young readers.

The heroine here answers to the nickname Berry. Chapters bring her friend Mollie Bragg, school days, and a cabin party. A girl named Lily tells her story, and a witch's tree adds a thrill. Berry lands in danger, guards a post, and takes a midnight adventure. Curtis sets a girl's home life against the great battle of Shiloh.
61342-a-white-king-in-east-africa-the-re:
John Boyes wrote his own remarkable adventures in East Africa, edited by Bulpett and printed at New York in 1912 with twelve illustrations and a map. Boyes, trader and soldier of fortune, became king of the Wa Kikuyu. He gives the book to William Northrop McMillan in memory of many tramps together. The following pages describe a life of adventure in the more remote parts of Africa, the editor begins.

These are adventures such as the explorer and sportsman do not generally encounter. The man has been personally known to me for some years, Bulpett vouches. In the days of travel and discovery, when Captain Cook and such heroes lived, such episodes were perhaps common enough. But every year the opportunities of such adventure get more and more remote. Boyes tells of trade, war, and kingship among the Kikuyu from his own mouth.
67098-winnie-the-pooh:
Winnie the Pooh is the famed child book of Milne, of a bear of small brain and his friends in a wood. This form was printed in Canada in the mid age, in its first print at Toronto. A list at its front names its hands past books for the young and for grown folk.

That list holds his verse book for the young, praised there as the best of its kind ever writ. Songs from that book, with tunes by a named hand and draws by its famed brush, stand there as well. His essays and a crime tale fill the grown list. Its gift word is short: hand in hand we come, its boy and his dad say, to lay this book at her feet.
67592-the-residuary-legatee-or-the-posth:
The Residuary Legatee, or the Posthumous Jest of the late John Austin, is a tale by Stimson, put out at New York in eighteen eighty eight. The rights were held in the two years that end in that year. The same hand's list of tales stands at the front of the print. The book is built in a strange frame: five acts, each named for a step in the work of a will.

The first act is the will, the next the add note to it, the third the rule of the dead man's goods. The fourth is the last counts, and the fifth the share that is left past all set gifts. In those acts the parts bear the names of the great love pairs of old tale.
a-publisher-and-his-friends-memoir-and-c: Samuel Smiles traces the house of John Murray in this memoir and correspondence, covering the origin and progress of the firm from 1768 to 1843. Condensed and edited by Thomas Mackay, the volume opens with the elder John Murray, formerly an officer of marines, who bought Sandby's business and began publishing. Later chapters follow the second John Murray, called the Anax of Publishers, through partnerships, quarrels, and the building of a great house.
britannica-1911-damoh:
Damoh is a town and district of British India in the Jubbulpore division of the Central Provinces. The town has a railway station 48 miles east of Saugor. Its people numbered 13,355 in 1901. A large cattle-market serves it, with small trades in weaving, dyeing, and pottery. The district around it covers 2,816 square miles. Open plains of mixed fertility fill most of it, broken by low hills and jungle in the south and east.

All the streams of Damoh flow from south to north, the Sunar and Bairma chief among them. Little use has been made of them for watering crops, though many spots would allow it. The district was formed in 1861, and its people fell by 12 percent in a decade through famine. The famine of 1896 to 1897 hit it hard, while that of 1900 was little felt. A branch railway from Saugor to Katni opened in January 1899.
britannica-1911-safed-koh:
Safed Koh, the white mountain wall of India, is ranged in a land entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The range runs on the north-west frontier like a straight wall. It towers fourteen thousand feet above the hills at its feet. It runs from the Kabul hills down toward the Indian border. Its strike cuts across the grain of the frontier ridges there.

Sikaram, its high peak, tops fifteen thousand six hundred feet. Yet that peak does not stand out on the straight-backed range. The Kabul River cuts the one deep gap through its line. That gap parts the Khyber route from the Kurram valley lands. No workable pass crosses the rough crest of the range. Woods cloak the west slopes, while south cliffs bake bare.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-merneptah-i-p:
Merneptah I, fourth king of Egypt's nineteenth dynasty and the supposed Pharaoh of the Exodus, reigned about 1234 to 1214 B.C. He was the thirteenth son of Rameses II, whom he succeeded in or about 1234, already long past middle age. His rule lasted some twenty years, with much building in the Delta, notably at Tanis, or Zoan, where he seized a number of his predecessors' monuments. 

 In his third year he crushed a revolt to the north-east, perhaps stirred by Hittites, and in his fifth year he repelled a Libyan invasion with allies. That victory is carved on a black granite stela found in 1896 in his funeral temple at Thebes, bearing the earliest known reference to Israel. He is commonly taken as the Exodus Pharaoh. Rameses II founded the cities Exodus says the oppressed Hebrews built, while Exodus implies his immediate successor reigned when Moses returned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-roh:
Peter Roh was a Swiss Jesuit preacher and teacher, born at Conthey in Valais in 1811. French-speaking until thirteen, he learned German from a nearby priest before Jesuit schooling at Brig and Sitten. Reading Pascal's Monita Secreta moved him to enter the Society in 1829. Clear, convincing teaching and a rare gift for oratory marked him early and fixed his double calling.

He taught dogmatics at Fribourg from 1842 and at the new Jesuit academy at Lucerne, preaching and aiding missions between lectures. The Sonderbund war made him a military chaplain, and its defeat drove him through Piedmont, Linz, and Gries to refuge as a tutor at Rappoltsweiler until 1849. From 1850 the people's missions in Germany became his true field, as he put it, his element. He died at Bonn in 1872.
